[Collections](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/List_of_Alexander_McQueen_collections#Collections)[Notes](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/List_of_Alexander_McQueen_collections#Notes)[References](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/List_of_Alexander_McQueen_collections#References)[Bibliography](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/List_of_Alexander_McQueen_collections#Bibliography) [](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_Alexander_McQueen_collections&action=edit§ion=0&oldformat=true)British designer [Alexander McQueen](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Alexander_McQueen "Alexander McQueen") designed 36 womenswear collections under his eponymous [fashion label](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Alexander_McQueen_/(brand/) "Alexander McQueen (brand)") during a career that lasted from 1992 until his death in 2010.[\[a\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/List_of_Alexander_McQueen_collections#cite_note-3)[\[3\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/List_of_Alexander_McQueen_collections#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWilson20155,_350%E2%80%93351-4) As a designer, McQueen was known for sharp [tailoring](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Tailoring "Tailoring"), [historicism](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Historicism_/(art/) "Historicism (art)"), and imaginative designs that often verged into the controversial.[\[4\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/List_of_Alexander_McQueen_collections#cite_note-BBCSixWays-5) His [runway shows](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Fashion_show "Fashion show") were known for being dramatic and theatrical, with some including elements of [performance art](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Performance_art "Performance art").[\[5\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/List_of_Alexander_McQueen_collections#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGleason201210-6)[\[6\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/List_of_Alexander_McQueen_collections#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFairerWilcox201613-7) McQueen drew inspiration for his clothing and shows from a broad range of sources, including [film](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Film "Film"), [history](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/History "History"), [nature](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Nature "Nature"), [world religions](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/World_religions "World religions"), [art](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Art "Art"), and his own life.[\[12\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/List_of_Alexander_McQueen_collections#cite_note-13) Through his work, he explored themes such as romanticism, sexuality, and death.[\[13\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/List_of_Alexander_McQueen_collections#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrankel201113%E2%80%9314-14)[\[14\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/List_of_Alexander_McQueen_collections#cite_note-15) [![Image 2: Thumb](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c5/Coat_made_of_silk%2C_Alexander_McQueen%2C_Savage_Beauty.jpg/250px-Coat_made_of_silk%2C_Alexander_McQueen%2C_Savage_Beauty.jpg)](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/List_of_Alexander_McQueen_collections#/media/File:Coat_made_of_silk,_Alexander_McQueen,_Savage_Beauty.jpg) [Frock coat](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Frock_coat "Frock coat") from graduation collection, _[Jack the Ripper Stalks His Victims](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Jack_the_Ripper_Stalks_His_Victims "Jack the Ripper Stalks His Victims")_ (1992) [![Image 3: Thumb](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6d/A_dress_by_Alexander_McQueen%2C_Savage_Beauty_at_V%26A.jpg/250px-A_dress_by_Alexander_McQueen%2C_Savage_Beauty_at_V%26A.jpg)](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/List_of_Alexander_McQueen_collections#/media/File:A_dress_by_Alexander_McQueen,_Savage_Beauty_at_V&A.jpg) Dress from unfinished final collection _[Angels and Demons](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Angels_and_Demons_/(collection/) "Angels and Demons (collection)")_ (Autumn/Winter 2010) He used unusual cuts and silhouettes to play with the human form, making wearers appear inhuman.[\[15\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/List_of_Alexander_McQueen_collections#cite_note-16) Early in his career, he originated an extreme low-rise trouser cut called the "[bumster](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Bumster "Bumster")", which became a brand signature.[\[16\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/List_of_Alexander_McQueen_collections#cite_note-FOOTNOTEThomas2015106,_115-17) Other significant designs include the skull scarf, another brand signature; the [oyster dress](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Oyster_dress "Oyster dress"); and the [armadillo shoe](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Armadillo_shoe "Armadillo shoe"), notably worn by singer [Lady Gaga](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Lady_Gaga "Lady Gaga").[\[17\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/List_of_Alexander_McQueen_collections#cite_note-FOOTNOTEThomas2015326,_338-18)[\[18\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/List_of_Alexander_McQueen_collections#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBethune2015321-19)[\[19\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/List_of_Alexander_McQueen_collections#cite_note-20) Womenswear was the focus of McQueen's career. In his early collections, he sometimes presented menswear or had male models walk in the shows, but his label did not have a regular menswear line until 2004.[\[20\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/List_of_Alexander_McQueen_collections#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBethune2015308-21)[\[21\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/List_of_Alexander_McQueen_collections#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWatt201287,_213-22) From October 1996 to October 2001, McQueen was – in addition to his responsibilities for his own label – head designer at French fashion house [Givenchy](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Givenchy "Givenchy"), for which he produced both [haute couture](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Haute_couture "Haute couture") and [ready-to-wear](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Ready-to-wear "Ready-to-wear") collections each season.[\[8\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/List_of_Alexander_McQueen_collections#cite_note-V&A_intro-9)[\[22\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/List_of_Alexander_McQueen_collections#cite_note-FOOTNOTEThomas2015209,_213-23)[\[23\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/List_of_Alexander_McQueen_collections#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWilson2015173%E2%80%93174,_255-24) This article concerns itself with McQueen's own-label womenswear collections. List of collections
CollectionSeasonShow dateShow locationThemes and inspirationNotes
Jack the Ripper Stalks His Victims1992 graduation collection16 March 1992[24][25]Duke of York's Headquarters, London[b][24][25]London serial killer Jack the Ripper and prostitution in the Victorian era, particularly their practice of selling locks of hair[30][31]Thesis collection for Master's degree in fashion at Central Saint Martins; purchased in its entirety by editor Isabella Blow[25]
Taxi DriverAutumn/Winter 1993March 1993[25]The Ritz Hotel, London[25]Taxi Driver, a 1976 neo-noir film by Martin Scorsese; to a lesser extent McQueen's taxi driver father[32][33]Debut of bumster trousers; exhibited rather than shown on runway;[c] no pieces survive as entire collection was accidentally lost immediately following the exhibit[34][16]
NihilismSpring/Summer 199418 October 1993[35]Bluebird Garage, London[35]Eclectic collection with no straightforward theme, elements of primitivism, pushback against feminine womenswear[36][37][38]First professional catwalk show[38]
BansheeAutumn/Winter 199426 February 1994[39]Café de Paris, London[1]The Gaelic banshee, a spirit whose wailing foretells death; darkly romanticised idea of resilience through tragedy[39]Isabella Blow walked as a model; show was reprised for New York Fashion Week at the behest of fashion promoter Derek Anderson[39][40]
The BirdsSpring/Summer 199510 September 1994[41]Bagley's warehouse, London[41]The Birds, a 1963 natural horror film by Alfred Hitchcock; ornithology; the mathematical designs of graphic artist M. C. Escher[42]First McQueen show styled by long-time collaborator Katy England[41]
Highland RapeAutumn/Winter 199513 March 1995[35]Natural History Museum, London[35]English violence towards Scotland, especially the Jacobite risings and the Highland Clearances[43]First critically-significant collection, led to 1996 hiring by Givenchy[43]
The HungerSpring/Summer 199623 October 1995[35]Natural History Museum, London[35]The Hunger, a 1983 erotic horror film featuring vampires[44]First time McQueen showed menswear; first show produced by Sam Gainsbury, who would produce every subsequent show[44]
DanteAutumn/Winter 19961 March 1996[45]Christ Church, Spitalfields, London[45]Religion and warfare; named for Dante's Inferno, a 14th-century epic poem describing Hell[44]First appearance of English supermodel Kate Moss in a McQueen show[44]
Bellmer La PoupéeSpring/Summer 199727 September 1996[45]Royal Horticultural Hall, London[45]Poupée, a 1934 series by surrealist photographer Hans Bellmer, which presented deconstructed dolls as a commentary on Nazi ideals[20]First show worked by Sarah Burton, who became McQueen's right-hand woman; Black model Debra Shaw walked while shackled to a metal frame, generating controversy[20]
It's a Jungle Out ThereAutumn/Winter 199727 February 1997[45]Borough Market, London[45]Life cycle of the Thomson's gazelle; savagery of the fashion industry; paintings by the Old Masters[20]Set accidentally caught fire during the show[20]
UntitledSpring/Summer 199828 September 1997[46]Gatliff Road Warehouse, London[46]Metamorphosis; brutality; contrast of McQueen's work at his own label and at Givenchy[47][48][49]Originally titled The Golden Shower in reference to the sex act and retitled after objections from sponsor American Express[47]
JoanAutumn/Winter 199825 February 1998[46]Gatliff Road Warehouse, London[46]Martyrdom and persecution in the medieval era, especially that of French folk heroine and saint Joan of Arc[47]McQueen was photographed for The Face magazine in April 1998 in hair and makeup similar to that used in this show[50]
No. 13Spring/Summer 199927 September 1997[46]Gatliff Road Warehouse, London[46]Arts and Crafts movement of the 1880s to 1920s; finale inspired by Rebecca Horn installation High Moon (1991)[51]Show ended with model Shalom Harlow being spray-painted by robots[51]
The OverlookAutumn/Winter 199923 February 1999[52]Gatliff Road Warehouse, London[52]The Shining, a 1980 psychological horror film by Stanley Kubrick, particularly its winter setting[51]First attendance of Vogue editor Anna Wintour at a McQueen show[53]
EyeSpring/Summer 200016 September 1999[54]Pier 94, New York City[52]Islamic culture and clothing, especially the burqa; relationship of Western world to Middle East[55]First time debuting a show outside of London[d][55]
EshuAutumn/Winter 200015 February 2000[55]Gainsborough Studios, London[55]Named for Yoruba deity Eshu; African-inspired primitivism with elements of Victorian fashion[55]Anti-fur activists broke into the venue before the show and vandalised the set, resulting in heavy security on the day of the show[57]
VossSpring/Summer 200126 September 2000[58]Gatliff Road Warehouse, London[58]Staged as a voyeuristic look inside a stereotypical insane asylum; dresses of unusual materials like seashells and microscope slides[58]Finale showpiece presented author Michelle Olley nude, masked, and covered with live moths, in a recreation of Sanitarium (1983), a photograph by Joel-Peter Witkin[58]
What a Merry-Go-RoundAutumn/Winter 200121 February 2001[52]Gatliff Road Warehouse, London[52]Dark underside of carnivals and circuses; Child Catcher villain from Chitty Chitty Bang Bang (1968)[58]Final presentation at Gatliff Road; first appearance of skull print that is now a signature of the brand[58]
The Dance of the Twisted BullSpring/Summer 20026 October 2001[59]Stade Français sports club (fr), Paris[59]Spanish culture, especially bullfighting and flamenco dancing[60]First collection after selling label to Gucci Group; first McQueen collection shown in Paris[60]
Supercalifragilistic-expialidociousAutumn/Winter 20029 March 2002[59]La Conciergerie, Paris[59]Films of American director Tim Burton, especially Sleepy Hollow (1990); English school uniforms; photography of Helmut Lang[60][61]Lighting and invitation by film director Tim Burton[62][63]
IrereSpring/Summer 20035 October 2002[59]Grande halle de la Villette, Paris[59]Three-phase narrative: shipwrecked pirates, drowned maidens in black, and birds of paradise[64]Debut of the "oyster dress", a riff on a 1987 design by John Galliano called the "shellfish dress"[65][66]
ScannersAutumn/Winter 20038 March 2003[67]Grande halle de la Villette, Paris[67]Journey eastward through the clothing of northern Eurasia: Siberia and the Russian Far East, Tibet, and Japan[64][68]Clear plastic wind tunnel was suspended over the runway for some models to walk through[69]
DeliveranceSpring/Summer 200410 October 2003[67]Salle Wagram, Paris[67]Depression-era fashion, 1969 film They Shoot Horses, Don't They?[70]Runway show was a performance emulating a dance marathon, with choreography by dancer Michael Clark[71]
Pantheon ad LucemAutumn/Winter 20045 March 2004[67]Grande halle de la Villette, Paris[67]Ancient Greek draped garments; science fiction films like Close Encounters of the Third Kind (1977) and 2001: A Space Odyssey (1968)[70]Entire title often incorrectly translated as Latin for "Towards the Light"; this is the correct translation for "ad lucem" but neglects to account for "pantheon"[70]
It's Only a GameSpring/Summer 20058 October 2004[72]Palais Omnisports de Paris-Bercy, Paris[72]Contrast of fashion cultures, giant chess scene from 2001 film of Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone[73]Runway show featured performance inspired by Harry Potter chess, choreographed by dancer Les Child[74]
The Man Who Knew Too MuchAutumn/Winter 20054 March 2005[72]Lycée Carnot, Paris[72]1950s fashion, particularly as seen in the Alfred Hitchcock thriller The Man Who Knew Too Much (1956)[73]Show invite based on theatrical poster for Hitchcock's film Vertigo (1958); first McQueen handbag, named for actress Kim Novak, who frequently appeared in Hitchcock films[73]
NeptuneSpring/Summer 20067 October 2005[75]Imprimerie Nationale, Paris[75]1980s fashion, including power dressing, hard glamour, and body conscious designs[76]All models were at least 5'11" in reference to the 1980s trend for Amazonian supermodels[77]
The Widows of CullodenAutumn/Winter 20063 March 2006[75]Palais Omnisports de Paris-Bercy, Paris[75]Second examination of English violence towards Scotland in more mature and melancholy terms; centres the widows of the Battle of Culloden (1746)[76]Show closed with an illusion of Kate Moss as an apparition within a glass pyramid at the centre of the stage[76]
SarabandeSpring/Summer 20076 October 2006[75]Cirque d'hiver, Paris[75]Exploration of fragility and decaying grandeur through floral motifs[78]One dress was covered with fresh flowers, which began to fall off on the runway in a moment of serendipitous beauty[79][80]
In Memory of Elizabeth Howe, Salem, 1692Autumn/Winter 20072 March 2007[81]Le Zénith Arena, Paris[81]Religious persecution conducted by Puritans in 17th century; ancient Egyptian religion; occult symbolism[78]Final McQueen show styled by long-time stylist Katy England[78]
La Dame BleueSpring/Summer 20085 October 2007[81]Palais Omnisports de Paris-Bercy, Paris[81]Reinvention through fashion; avian and butterfly motifs; personal style of Isabella Blow[82][83]Collaboration with Philip Treacy to memorialise their mutual friend Isabella Blow, who committed suicide in May 2007[82]
The Girl Who Lived in the TreeAutumn/Winter 200829 February 2008[84]Palais Omnisports de Paris-Bercy, Paris[81]Fairy tale narrative about a girl who lived in a tree; British culture and national symbols; clothing of India during the British Raj[82]Philip Treacy created a single headpiece for the collection: an enormous peacock with fanned tail, made from driftwood and sea fan coral[85]
Natural Dis-tinction Un-natural SelectionSpring/Summer 20093 October 2008[86]Le Centquatre, Paris[86]Beauty of nature contrasted with the impact of human industry[87]First of final three collections which shared a theme of the destruction of nature by humanity[88]
The Horn of PlentyAutumn/Winter 200910 March 2009[86]Palais Omnisports de Paris-Bercy, Paris[86]Dark satire of the fashion industry with pastiches of notable designers and McQueen's past works; many items made to resemble trash[87]Creative process documented by photographer Nick Waplington, published in photo book Alexander McQueen: Working Process[89]
Plato's AtlantisSpring/Summer 20106 October 2009[86]Palais Omnisports de Paris-Bercy, Paris[86]Human evolution following global flooding as a result of climate change[18]Final fully-realised collection; first livestreamed fashion show in history; debut of the armadillo shoe; debut of Lady Gaga single "Bad Romance"[18][90]
Angels and DemonsAutumn/Winter 201010 March 2010[18]Hôtel de Clermont-Tonnerre (fr), Paris[18]Religious paintings of the Medieval and Renaissance periods[18]Collection left incomplete at the time of McQueen's suicide in February 2010, completed posthumously by his assistant Sarah Burton; title is unofficial[18]

*   [Home](https://www.londonmuseum.org.uk/)
*   [Objects & Stories](https://www.londonmuseum.org.uk/collections/)
*   [London stories](https://www.londonmuseum.org.uk/collections/london-stories/)

![Image 1](https://media.londonmuseum.org.uk/images/WagtailSource-ALEXANDER-MCQUEEN.height-1200.format-webp.webp)

Alexander McQueen was a singular force in fashion. His collections were full of daringly original garments, which could be both rooted in tradition and totally severed from fashion conventions.

His creativity pushed beyond the bodily limits of clothing. He dressed models in corsets made of glass and aluminium coils, and took ‘low ride’ trousers down way below the hip.

McQueen grew up in working-class Stratford, in Newham. He mastered his craft in the workrooms of Savile Row and studio spaces on Hoxton Square. London is sewn right through McQueen’s garments, giving us a way to understand the city’s history, his heritage and how the two entangle.

McQueen was one of the leading fashion designers of the late 20th and early 21st century. He created 36 collections for his label, called Alexander McQueen, during his lifetime. From 1996 to 2001, he also designed for French luxury fashion house Givenchy. Many of his garments explored themes like sex, death, romanticism and history.

McQueen’s exceptional ability to create clothes that looked like works of art earned him huge success in the 1990s and 2000s. He won British Designer of the Year four times and was awarded Commander of the Order of the British Empire (CBE), a prestigious title given by the monarchy, in 2003.

McQueen died by suicide in 2010. His longtime collaborator Sarah Burton took over as creative director of his label after his death.

*   ![Image 2: A mannequin displays an elegant white dress with delicate floral patterns, featuring a gathered bodice and flowing asymmetrical skirt.](https://media.londonmuseum.org.uk/images/WagtailSource-2004_16-jpg.width-1136.format-webp.webp)
    
*   ![Image 3: A textile artwork featuring a stylized portrait of queen elizabeth ii against a background with the union jack.](https://media.londonmuseum.org.uk/images/WagtailSource-2009_76-tif.width-1136.format-webp.webp)
    

McQueen’s fashion foundations were laid in [Savile Row in Mayfair](https://www.londonmuseum.org.uk/collections/london-stories/savile-row-the-heart-of-london-tailoring/), the historic home of British high-end tailoring.

He left school at 16 to do a tailoring course at Newham College, working at his uncle’s pub on the side. Then he bagged himself two apprenticeships with tailors on the Row: first at Anderson & Sheppard, later at Gieves & Hawkes.

McQueen quickly picked up traditional tailoring techniques and pattern cutting, working a lot with historical and military clothing. Trained to cut cloth with speedy precision, he could create a garment seemingly out of thin air.

Savile Row gave him a grounding in fashion history – which he could later turn on its head. “Everything I do is based on tailoring,” he once said.

After a few years on Savile Row, McQueen spent a short time working on coats and waistcoats at London costumier Bermans & Nathans, which included making costumes for a production of _Les Misérables._

Aged 20, he worked as a pattern cutter for experimental designer Koji Tatsuno. He also worked on the fetishistic leather bondage collection for Ladbroke Grove-based fashion label Red or Dead.

In 1990, McQueen applied for a job at Central Saint Martins, London’s famous arts college, as a pattern-cutting tutor. Instead, the head of the masters course encouraged him to enrol as a student on the MA fashion course.

McQueen’s 1992 degree collection was called _Jack the Ripper Stalks His Victims_. It was inspired by the [five women murdered in Whitechapel in 1888](https://www.londonmuseum.org.uk/collections/london-stories/jack-ripper/) by an unknown serial killer named Jack the Ripper.

While police and journalists at the time labelled the victims ‘prostitutes’, only one, Mary Jane Kelly, was known to have worked in the sex trade. Still, this misinformation has followed the victims for over 100 years. The degree show notes described it as a “day into eveningwear collection inspired by 19th century street walkers”.

*   ![Image 4: Illustrated page from "police news" featuring multiple scenes related to whitechapel murders with a central portrait of a man, circa late 1800s.](https://media.londonmuseum.org.uk/images/WagtailSource-The-Illustrated-Po.width-1136.format-webp.webp)
    
*   ![Image 5](https://media.londonmuseum.org.uk/images/WagtailSource-28_88_2-tif.width-1136.format-webp.webp)
    
    This child’s [mourning hair bracelet](https://www.londonmuseum.org.uk/collections/v/object-284323/bracelet-mourning-bracelet/) is probably woven with the hair of a dead relative, perhaps a parent or sibling.
    

Putting his skilful cutting learned on the Row to good use, a number of McQueen’s garments drew on Victorian silhouettes, like corsets, bustles and frock coats.

He also stitched a lock of his hair into the linings of several items. Back in the 1800s, hair was exchanged between lovers and friends, or kept to mourn dead relatives, like the hairwork in [this mourning bracelet in our collection](https://www.londonmuseum.org.uk/collections/v/object-284323/bracelet-mourning-bracelet/).

> “We were all working for nothing because we needed to do it”
> 
> Alexander McQueen, 2007

McQueen launched his label in 1992, the same year he graduated. In 1993, he moved into a design studio in Hoxton Square, Shoreditch, where he worked on his collections with local creatives such as blacksmiths, glassblowers and welders.

“Everyone worked together at the beginning of the nineties,” he told [_Purple_ magazine](https://purple.fr/magazine/ss-2007-issue-7/alexander-mcqueen/). “We were all working for nothing because we needed to do it. Otherwise, there would be nothing in London.”

![Image 6: A person with a shaved head sits at a cluttered desk, holding papers and wearing a sleeveless black shirt, a tattoo visible on their upper arm.](https://media.londonmuseum.org.uk/images/WagtailSource-ALEXANDER-MCQUEEN-.width-1120.format-webp.webp)

Still from the 2018 film _McQueen._

The area was on the cusp of gentrification. Artists had been moving into this largely deprived part of east London since the late 1980s, making the most of cheap rent and empty warehouse spaces.

In 1993, [Young British Artists](https://www.londonmuseum.org.uk/collections/london-stories/who-were-the-young-british-artists/) Tracey Emin and Sarah Lucas set up their studio-come-shop The Shop on nearby Bethnal Green Road. The Blue Note opened on Hoxton Square the same year. The nightclub hosted trailblazing nights by drum and bass label Metalheadz and [dub](https://www.londonmuseum.org.uk/collections/london-stories/dub-london-shops-sound-systems-legends/) pioneer Aba Shanti, which started drawing adventurous clubbers east.

Mcqueen’s early years at Hoxton Square were hard graft. He worked on tight budgets, often with little money left over for himself. The London fashion scene wasn’t paying attention to the artistry and skill of his tailoring. “London gives me fuck all,” he said in 1993.

His breakthrough came in 1995 with his autumn/winter collection, _Highland Rape_. In 1996, McQueen won his first British Designer of the Year Award and became the chief designer of womenswear at Givenchy.

_Vanity Fair_ interviewed him in Hoxton Square in the wake of this newfound fame. The magazine’s March 1997 issue, ‘[London! Swings! Again!](https://www.londonmuseum.org.uk/collections/v/object-283789/vanity-fair-london-swings-again/)’, featured a gushing 25-page spread of the new names of “the Coolest City on Earth”.

*   ![Image 7: A vanity fair magazine cover featuring a man and a woman wrapped in a union jack flag with the headline "london swings again!.](https://media.londonmuseum.org.uk/images/WagtailSource-Vanity-Fair-London.width-1136.format-webp.webp)
    
*   ![Image 8: Collage of black-and-white photos depicting various public figures in events, with captions, in a magazine layout.](https://media.londonmuseum.org.uk/images/WagtailSource-Vanity-Fair-London.width-1136.format-webp_mPZ79T2.webp)
    
    McQueen is pictured in the middle walking down the runway at his “sensational fashion show".
    

McQueen is [framed by the article](https://archive.vanityfair.com/article/1997/3/london-swings-again), a little dismissively, as one of London’s new “provocateurs”. Formerly the “enfant terrible of London fashion,” he was now “the courtier to ladies who lunch and Argentinians with means… Not bad for the son of an East End [cabbie](https://www.londonmuseum.org.uk/collections/london-stories/hailing-history-london-black-cabs/)!”

> “anything I experience, I digest and then vomit back into society”
> 
> Alexander McQueen, 2003

McQueen was inspired by London and his family history
-----------------------------------------------------

McQueen’s influences were numerous: Victoriana, the Gothic, film, photography, taxidermy, to name a few. His family history, which stretched from the East End to Scotland, also strongly shaped his vision. “My work is biographical,” he said in an [interview with SHOWstudio](https://www.showstudio.com/projects/in_camera/in-camera-alexander-mcqueen-1), “so anything I experience, I digest and then vomit back into society.”

He was inspired by his mum’s work on her own family history, which was rooted in the East End. His research into Jack the Ripper for his degree show was sparked by her discovery that one of the victims stayed in their relative’s inn.

McQueen also learned from his mum that he descended from [Huguenot refugees](https://www.londonmuseum.org.uk/collections/london-stories/the-huguenots-london/) who moved to Spitalfields in the 1680s. In 1996, honouring this heritage, he presented his autumn/winter collection in the [dramatic Georgian architecture](https://www.londonmuseum.org.uk/collections/london-stories/londons-georgian-era-architecture/) of [Christ Church Spitalfields](https://www.londonmuseum.org.uk/collections/v/object-94068/christ-church-spitalfields/).

*   ![Image 9: Gray tailored suit with decorative studs on the jacket and pants, displayed on a mannequin against a white background.](https://media.londonmuseum.org.uk/images/WagtailSource-2003_73_va-tif.width-1136.format-webp.webp)
    
    Wool and cashmere [trouser suit](https://www.londonmuseum.org.uk/collections/v/object-729350/suit/) designed by Alexander McQueen for his spring/summer ready-to-wear collection, 2003.
    
*   ![Image 10: A black traditional suit adorned with intricate gold and floral embroidery, displayed on a mannequin against a white background.](https://media.londonmuseum.org.uk/images/WagtailSource-63_7-tif_6B9s2LV.width-1136.format-webp.webp)
    

This wool and cashmere suit from 2003 is part of our collection. It points to another aspect of living East End history: [pearly kings and queens](https://www.londonmuseum.org.uk/collections/london-stories/who-are-pearly-kings-queens/). McQueen sewed mother-of-pearl buttons onto the hip of the trousers, just as London’s charitable cockney royalty have covered their clothes in buttons since the late 1800s.

Documenting McQueen: Tailoring

Unearthing the origins of the signature codes and stories that define the house, brought to life through the McQueen archive.

### Episode 2: ‘Deliverance’ McQueen Spring Summer 2004

Alistair O’Neill, Professor of Fashion at London's Central Saint Martins School of Art and Design, explores pieces from the McQueen Archive.

The Spring Summer 2004 ‘Deliverance’ collection, reveals the storytelling and techniques established by Lee Alexander McQueen that still echo through the house today.

Watch the film to discover how the Spring Summer 2004 collection continues to inspire the house's signature tailoring.

Pieces:

Look 11: Tailored fishtail dress in silk taffeta and cotton twill with ostrich feather underskirt.

Look 33: Tailored jacket and skirt in Prince of Wales wool with intarsia silk organza inserts and lace hem.

Look 95: Tailored skirt in Prince of Wales wool with multi-patterned floral appliqué and patchwork details.

Sandals in embossed leather with watch face detailing.

Captured by Chanel Moye. Music by Joss Davy.

### Episode 1: ‘Dante’ McQueen Autumn Winter 1996

Alistair O’Neill, renowned historian and Professor at London's Central Saint Martins School of Art and Design, explores the depths of the McQueen archive, tracing the foundations of definitively McQueen codes, beginning with tailoring.

Examining pieces from the Autumn Winter 1996 ‘Dante’ collection, O'Neill reveals the storytelling underpinning Lee Alexander McQueen's signature precision, rooted in McQueen’s Savile Row training.

Watch the film to discover how McQueen’s foundational techniques continue to define the house's subversive spirit.

Pieces:

Look 1: Tailored dress in black wool with sheer tulle inserts. Guinea fowl claw earrings. Buckled French court shoe in black leather.

Look 33: Tailored jacket with peaked lapels and button details in black cotton twill.

Captured by Chanel Moye. Music by Joss Davy.

40.content:
**From the British tailor, tragically deceased in 2010, we keep in mind the spectacular creations and the head spinning heel-turns. But Alexander McQueen was first a true technician of the fabric. As he should be: between his 16 and 18 years, he learned the ropes at the illustrious tailor Anderson & Sheppard… Let us look back to a relatively unknown but key period in the creator’s life.**

_By Gino Delmas, in London._  
_Article originally published in L'Etiquette issue 3._

Him over there? Alexander McQueen from Anderson & Sheppard? The sentence doesn’t make sense. Neither does the union. On one side, a shooting star, on the other, a monumental institution. Modernity and creativity versus tradition and know-how. At Anderson & Sheppard’s, on endless bookshelves, are piled up threads of fine fabric and receipts from the firm’s customers. Cary Grant, Gary Cooper, Charlie Chaplin or Fred Astaire have been here. Prince Charles, Martin Scorsese and Brian Ferry are regulars. So do Calvin Klein and Tom Ford. Here, we promise to never change a thing, to offer always the same suit, always the best. For Alexander McQueen, the obsession was quite the opposite. A collection had to wipe the previous one clean in creative whirlwind positively out of control. His inspirations? Jack the Ripper, then Hitchcock’s The Birds, then Kubrick’s the Shining, then war. Provocative? Constantly. One season, the Britton directed on the catwalk derelict women, ‘raped women,’ was his justification. Another one, he had robots directly spray-paint his models’ dresses on. Alexander McQueen at Anderson & Sheppard? The alliance made no sense. And yet, it did happen. Between the age of 16 and 18, the lad that everyone then called ‘Lee’ learned how to tailor a suit in the honourable firm. A mere anecdote? No, the cornerstone of his career.

FOCUS, GIFTED, QUICK

The story begins in the Spring of 1985. Lee is 16-years-old, he had just left school, with no training, no prospect. For a few months he attends night classes At West Ham Technical College. Next to stay-at-home moms and wannabe artists, he learns the basics of drawing. In a Pub of his neighbourhood, in Stratford, in East London, Lee sometimes earns a few quids serving pie & mash to the local workers. The rest of the time, the teenager listens to house music, goes through piles of books on ornithology, which fascinates him, and peruse the few fashion magazine that go through his hands. Lee feels the creative type, but isn’t again the idea of watching TV, lounging on the couch of the modest family home on Biggerstaff Road. One day, the BBC happens to show a feature on Savile Row. Subdued ambience. Striped flannels. Tailor’s scissors. The documentary praises the English know-how but worries about the lack of workers. Prestigious London tailor shops are desperately looking for apprentices. Joyce, Lee’s mother, a social science teacher, is sitting on the coach next to him. For her, it clicks immediately. Why not go? Why not try his luck?For once, Lee isn’t against the idea of trying. Lucky, since his father, a cabbie, exasperated by his son’s laziness, does not give him much of a choice…

A few days later, there he is on Savile Row, dressed in his usual baggy jeans and his everlasting black Doc Martens. But what door to knock on, without any contact or leg up? On instinct, he heads for Anderson & Sheppard, the biggest name, the one he heard most through the years. Lucky shot. The tailor is looking for workers, and the current policy is to recruit young people without any formal training nor experience, more likely to learn the house’s ways quickly. Lee is asked to come back three days later. On that day, at the hour set, he climbs to the third store and sets his stuff on a large wooden table, marked by both time and scissors cut. It is divided in four spaces, each an assigned working station. Lorraine and Wendy, two other apprentices, have been working here for a few months already. The last corner is occupied by Cornelius O’Callaghan, a fifty-something Irishman strict and silent, whom everybody calls ‘Con.’ He’s one of the best tailor in the house and probably one of the best in London. ‘Con was a historical figure of Anderson & Sheppard,’ remembers Rose Mary, now in charge of vests. ‘He was part of a generation which learn tailoring right after the war. He had the rigour and discipline of this generation that went through the army or the marine. With him, you had to work and shut up.’ Without delay, Con gives young Lee a thimble, some needles and some threads.

Lee already know the basics of sewing, having learned with his mother and his sister Janet. For the latter, he had even already made several outfits, including a black tube dress. ‘So tight that I could hardly move my legs to walk up the stairs, but everybody kept complementing me when I was wearing it,’ says she. But his technical knowledge is limited, and tailoring, the art of making a suit, is for him a whole new universe. So, with application, he set out to work. The first lesson is about the inside of the jacket’s lapel. Lee learns. The days start at 8:30am and end at 5pm. One pause for tea in the morning, one in the afternoon, and a few minutes for lunch, usually a sandwich eaten on the corner of the table. Like the other apprentices in the firm, Lee earns 30 pounds a week. ‘It was something out of Dickens, legs folded on a bench, making lapels,’ he would sum up to the BBC in 1997.

![Image 1](https://cdn.shopify.com/s/files/1/0552/3865/6195/products/Capture_d_ecran_2023-01-16_a_12.59.28.png?v=1673871331)

Lee is an apprentice both hard-working and talented. ‘He was very focused, he wanted to learn how to make a jacket, and quickly. He had this latent determination,’ remembers Byron, now in charge of fitting pants at the tailor. ‘He had a real thirst for knowledge,’ confirms Derrick, another apprentice, present at the same time as McQueen. The results are coming to fruition. After the inside of the lapel, the young man learns interfacing, the inner pockets, then the outside of the lapel. At Anderson & Sheppard, it is considered normal for an apprentice starting from zero to learn to make a forward, an almost finished jacket, ready for the first fitting with the customer, in four years. Three at the most. But Lee reaches this point after only two years. He has mastered the characteristic Anderson & Sheppard shoulder, a supple shoulder with a high armhole, recognisable to this small surplus of fabric forming delicate folds and giving the impression of a larger breast and thinner waist. McQueen’s dexterity is such that sounds he sets up jackets destined to the firm’s most prestigious clients, like Prince Charles or Calvin Klein. ‘I was quick, I was good,’ he’ll brag to the BBC.

TECHNICAL, CREATIVE

Later, throughout his career, McQueen will always be noticed for his technical dexterity. In October 1990, when he joins the Masters of Design of Saint Martins, the famous London fashion school, he is the only one without degree, but also the only one able to completely cut and fit a model. At the time, his friend Alice Smith is used to purchasing fabric for him at the Berwick Street market. Lee spreads the fabric on the floor of his tiny apartment of Primrose Hill, and the magic happens. ‘He had a great pair of scissors given to him by his aunt, and he would cut without template or markers, and it would be perfect every time… I could not believe it.’ In front of a model or a fabric, Lee is never intimidated. In 1996, at a fitting day for Givenchy, a few days before his first show for the company, Eva Herzigova shows up in a tight fitting suit. But something is off. In front of the shocked eyes of the head of the workshop, who had spent hours working on the piece, Lee grabs a pair of scissors and cuts both legs to make it a body. The scissors are a tool to deconstruct, but also to build: it’s what he does in front of the camera of the journalist Marie-Christiane Marek, in 1997: from a large white fabric, McQueen, a pair of scissors in hand and nothing more, shapes a shoulder on a Stockman. Another example? A few years later, the Brit works on the costumes for the ballet Eonnagata. The first ballerina Sylvie Guillem did not forget it. ‘Alexander had among other things made a costume for a character that was black and negative. At the fitting, he did not find it sinister enough. He said: “bring me scissors and fabric” and there, in front of us, he made another costume. It took about three minutes. So quick, and in end perfect.’

With McQueen, through the years and the fashion shows, his mastery of the suit will remain a key element. ‘Everything I do is based on tailoring,’ the creator used to repeat. ‘Anderson & Sheppard gave Lee this platform to go where he wanted to go. He built his silhouettes on theoretical and practical bases,’ explains his nephew Gary McQueen, who has long worked alongside him. En 1992, the star object of his end of the year exhibition at Saint Martins, is a spectacular jacket. Cut in a jet-black fabric, it is short, flared on the mid rift. The interfacing is made with human hair. Here’s the recipe. Perfect tailoring, creative madness. On his first shows, McQueen insists we wear a new cut of pants, the bumster, so low cut he partly covers the pubis and reveals the top of the rear. Later, there’ll be the squared and straight shoulders of the VOSS collection in 2001, then those large of the ruthless bankers of The Forgotten in 2007. In 2010, for his last male show, a few months before taking his own life, McQueen will decide for ‘pagoda shoulders,’ going up high, like the roofs of pagodas.

DISCREET, SILENT, PROVOCATIVE

At Anderson & Sheppard, through the years, we observed with growing curiosity the trajectory of this young man. ‘I wondered how he went from a young apprentice specialised in jackets to a designer who imagined such fantastical creations,’ still wonders Frances, an apprentice at the same period as Lee. ‘I could never have predicted that he had all this within himself, this entire universe.’ One must say that, in the workshop, Lee was the discreet sort. ‘He didn’t socialise much with the other apprentices,’ remembers Danny, another apprentice of the time at Anderson & Sheppard and now their head cutter. Conversations are rare, furtive. When Con takes a break, Lorraine and Wendy sometime tease Lee about his clothes or his musical tastes. One day, at tea time, the conversation escalates. The young women know nothing of house music. They don’t understand how anyone could like it. Or pretend not to understand. Lee attempts to explain. Derrick joins in the conversation: ‘I took his side and from then on there was a strong connection,’ laughs the only one who was close to Lee during his apprenticeship. ‘We were the only people in the firm to like house music. We talked about it whenever we could.’

Lee doesn’t live his 501 nor his Doc Martens. He often wears a black turtleneck, an oxford shirt, or a squared jacket. Through the months, as his technical mastery grows, he seems to refine his tastes, his vision of clothing. More and more, during the lunch break, he drafts discreetly drawings or dresses. Sometimes, too, Lee goes away for a few minutes, then a few hours. Does he go, as he say, take care of Jouye, his sick mother? Or does he simply have something better to do. Lee is now 18, he goes out more and more and discovers the pleasures of the night with groups of friends. Sometimes he is euphoric. Other times, he seems caught up by his demons. The difficulty to plainly live his homosexuality, and have his father accept it, weighs heavily on him. The memory of sexual abuse committed by the first husband of his older sister Janet while he was only 9-years-old haunt him. ‘We were started to feel some torment brewing inside him,’ believe Frances. A form of distance sets between himself and Anderson & Sheppard. It is actually at that time that Lee decides to let a wild rumour run loose. He tells his colleagues that he wrote some poorly-chosen words on the lining of one of Prince Charles’ jackets. He swears, insists, and amuse himself by observing the mortified looks on his colleague’s face. For years, he amuses himself by keeping the rumour going. Up to a point where Anderson & Sheppard will eventually recall the jacket in question to check the lining: nothing. Merely a provocation.

After two years, halfway to his apprenticeship, Lee leaves Anderson & Sheppard. He leaves without a diploma but with his head held high. ‘When he left, he told me: “one day, I’ll have my own business”’ remembers Byron, the head of adjustments for pants of the tailor shop. ‘In another conversation, he even told another tailor that one day he’d have a firm on Savile Row. He wasn’t even 20-years-old. We all laughed when we heard that.’ In 2013, three years after his death, a McQueen shop did open on Savile Row. ‘Letting him go was a blessing for him, he wasn’t made for that world,’ says Frances. ‘There’s a lot of talent in our shop, but his ambition wouldn’t have been satisfied making the same piece all his life… I think his time here showed him what he didn’t want to do,’ she explains, sitting at her workshop. In 1997, to the BBC mic, the man in question would have this phrase who would keep resonating: ‘I wouldn’t have survived in a place like that, closed up in a workshop fixing lapels…’

_To watch (absolutely) ‘McQueen’, by Ian Bonhôte and Peter Ettedgui, 2018._

British designer Lee Alexander McQueen (b. March 17, 1969, in Lewisham, London; † February 11, 2010, in London) entered the fashion world as an enfant terrible for his eccentric, sometimes scandalous fashion shows. The designer's trademarks include extremely low-slung hipsters, a stylized skull and crossbones, and recurring futuristic-evolutionary and darkly morbid elements. Along with John Galliano and Vivienne Westwood, McQueen is considered one of the most important British fashion designers of his time — a visionary, revolutionary, and provocateur of the international fashion industry.

![Image 1: Portrait of Alexander McQueen](https://wunderlabel.com/assets/information-pages/images/bios/alexander-mcqueen/alexander-mcqueen-portrait.png?1763380151)

Portrait of Alexander McQueen created with [Midjourney](https://www.midjourney.com/)

Vita
----

*   After tailoring clothes for his sisters at a young age of 16 (1985), McQueen left school and trained as a men's tailor with the traditional tailors Anderson & Sheppard and Gieves & Hawkes on Mayfair's Savile Row in London.
    
*   ### 1989
    
    At 20, McQueen started working as a pattern cutter for Japanese designer Koji Tatsuno. He then moved to Milan to work for Italian designer Romeo Gigli. This was followed by jobs as a theater costume designer in London and with Italian fashion designer Romeo Gigli in Milan.
    
*   ### 1992
    
    McQueen graduated from Central Saint Martins College of Art and Design in London with a Master of Arts degree. The British Vogue stylist Isabella Blow buys his entire graduation collection. Since that day Isabella was considered his muse and mentor.
    
    ![Image 2: Central Saint Martins College of Art and Design](https://wunderlabel.com/assets/information-pages/images/bios/alexander-mcqueen/central-saint-martins-college-of-art-and-design.svg?1763380151)
    
    Central Saint Martins College of Art and Design
    
*   ### 1993
    
    The designer founded the fashion company Alexander McQueen Trading Limited, with headquarters in Haywards Heath. In the early years he exclusively created women's collections, which, like his later works, were always inspired by his own autobiography and a fascination with the animal kingdom.
    
    ![Image 3: Alexander McQueen's Nihilism Collection](https://wunderlabel.com/assets/information-pages/images/bios/alexander-mcqueen/nihilism-collection.svg?1763380151)
    
    Alexander McQueen's Nihilism Collection
    
*   ### 1996
    
    McQueen received the British Designer of the Year award from the British Fashion Awards for the first time. He wins the title again in 1997, 2001 and 2003. He becomes head designer of Givenchy.
    
    ![Image 4](https://wunderlabel.com/assets/information-pages/images/bios/alexander-mcqueen/british-designer-of-the-year-award.svg?1763380151)
    
    British Designer of the Year Award
    
*   ### 1997
    
    McQueen succeeds John Galliano as haute couture designer for the Givenchy fashion house.
    
*   ### 1999
    
    McQueen opens his first boutique.
    
*   ### 2000
    
    McQueen marries documentary filmmaker George Forsyth. His maid of honor is none other than Kate Moss. However, the separation of the couple follows just one year later.
    
*   ### 2001
    
    McQueen's company has belonged to the Gucci Group of the French luxury goods group Kering (known as PPR until 2013), after McQueen signs over 51% of his shares to the group. In the process, he also loses his job at Givenchy, but remains creative director of his own brand.
    
*   ### 2003–2004
    
    With the turn of the millennium, the designer expands to New York and Milan and for the first time designs a men's collection (2004) and also fragrances (2003). He was named International Designer of the Year by the Council of Fashion Designers in 2003.
    
    ![Image 5](https://wunderlabel.com/assets/information-pages/images/bios/alexander-mcqueen/alexander-mcqueens-parfum-and-my-queen-eau-de-parfum.svg?1763380151)
    
    Alexander McQueen's _Parfum_ and _My Queen Eau de Parfum_
    
*   ### 2005
    
    McQueen begins a collaboration with Puma.
    
    ![Image 6: McQueen Street Climb Puma Sneaker](https://wunderlabel.com/assets/information-pages/images/bios/alexander-mcqueen/mcqueen-street-climb-puma-sneaker.svg?1763380151)
    
    McQueen Street Climb Puma Sneaker
    
*   ### 2006
    
    McQueen designs a large part of the outfits for Lady Gaga. Madonna, Courtney Love and David Bowie also wear McQueen's clothes on stage.
    
*   ### 2010
    
    In February 2010 fashion designer Alexander McQueen is found dead in his apartment the day before his mother's funeral. An autopsy reveals that he consumed a cocktail of drugs and then hanged himself.
    
*   After McQueen's death, designer Sarah Burton, McQueen's right-hand woman since 1996, continues to run the Alexander McQueen brand. Burton designed the wedding dress for Kate Middleton, helping the McQueen brand become even more famous worldwide.
    
*   ### 2011
    
    The Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York City hosted a highly popular posthumous exhibition of McQueen's work in 2011 titled Savage Beauty, featuring elaborate staging with unique architectural finishes and soundtracks for each room. The retrospective of his work becomes one of the most visited exhibitions of the museum ever.
    

Trivia
------

*   The British Fashion Council named McQueen British Designer of the Year four times between 1996 and 2001.
*   McQueen's fashion shows are always artistically choreographed, technically staged and repeatedly marked by scandals such as models covered in blood and people with prosthetic legs, exposed breasts and references to Joan of Arc, Jack the Ripper or Taxi Driver.
*   Lady Gaga releases the song "Fashion of his love" about McQueen after his death.

### Sources

**Daphne Diana Joan Susanna Guinness** (born 9 November 1967) is an English fashion designer, socialite, actress, film producer, and musician.

Her father is [Jonathan Guinness, 3rd Baron Moyne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonathan_Guinness,_3rd_Baron_Moyne "Jonathan Guinness, 3rd Baron Moyne"), the eldest son of [Diana Mitford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diana_Mitford "Diana Mitford") and [Bryan Guinness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryan_Guinness,_2nd_Baron_Moyne "Bryan Guinness, 2nd Baron Moyne"). Diana Mitford was the daughter of [David Freeman-Mitford, 2nd Baron Redesdale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Freeman-Mitford,_2nd_Baron_Redesdale "David Freeman-Mitford, 2nd Baron Redesdale"), the father of the [Mitford sisters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mitford_sisters "Mitford sisters"). Mitford divorced Guinness and married the leader of the British Union of Fascists, [Sir Oswald Mosley, 6th Baronet of Ancoats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oswald_Mosley "Oswald Mosley"). Daphne Guinness has said she did not know of Mosley's political affiliations, before she heard in 1980 on the [BBC News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC_News "BBC News") that he had died.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daphne_Guinness#cite_note-garratt-1)

As a child, Guinness grew up moving between the country houses owned by her family in England and Ireland, and a villa in Spain, where [Salvador Dalí](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salvador_Dal%C3%AD "Salvador Dalí") was a family friend.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daphne_Guinness#cite_note-2) She later lived in New York with her half-sister, [Catherine Guinness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catherine_Guinness "Catherine Guinness"), who was working as a Personal Assistant to [Andy Warhol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andy_Warhol "Andy Warhol").[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daphne_Guinness#cite_note-3)

Guinness has been a fashion model,[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daphne_Guinness#cite_note-NewYorker-4) a curator,[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daphne_Guinness#cite_note-NPRJackiLyden-5) and fashion writer.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daphne_Guinness#cite_note-FTSolowij-6) [Christian Allaire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christian_Allaire "Christian Allaire") of _[Vogue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vogue_/(magazine/) "Vogue (magazine)")_ referred to her as a "street style icon, producer, musician, and muse of [Alexander McQueen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_McQueen "Alexander McQueen") and [Karl Lagerfeld](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Lagerfeld "Karl Lagerfeld")".[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daphne_Guinness#cite_note-VogueAllaire-7) Guinness has been described as a "performance artist" by _[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_York_Times "The New York Times")_ for her use of and experimentation with fashion.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daphne_Guinness#cite_note-NYTTrebay-8) She has appeared on the covers of multiple international editions of _Vogue_,[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daphne_Guinness#cite_note-NewYorker-4)[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daphne_Guinness#cite_note-NBCVogue-9) _[Harper's Bazaar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harper%27s_Bazaar "Harper's Bazaar")_,[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daphne_Guinness#cite_note-FashionSpot-10) _[Tatler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tatler "Tatler")_, _[Zoo Magazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zoo_Magazine "Zoo Magazine")_, and other fashion magazines.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daphne_Guinness#cite_note-DesignScene-11)[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daphne_Guinness#cite_note-Sidewalk-12)

Guinness has written numerous pieces on the topic of fashion,[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daphne_Guinness#cite_note-FTSolowij-6) including columns published in _Vogue_,[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daphne_Guinness#cite_note-VogueGuinnness-13) the _[Financial Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Financial_Times "Financial Times")_,[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daphne_Guinness#cite_note-14) _[The Times of London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Times "The Times")_,[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daphne_Guinness#cite_note-TheTimes-15) and _Harper's Bazaar_.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daphne_Guinness#cite_note-16)[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daphne_Guinness#cite_note-17) She also wrote the foreword to _Alexander McQueen: Fashion Visionary,_[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daphne_Guinness#cite_note-18) contributed to _Dressed to Kill: Jazz Age Fashion,_[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daphne_Guinness#cite_note-19) and co-authored _Art/Fashion in the 21st Century._[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daphne_Guinness#cite_note-20) As a designer, Guinness has designed a collection of shirts with [Comme des Garçons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comme_des_Gar%C3%A7ons "Comme des Garçons") for [Dover Street Market](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dover_Street_Market "Dover Street Market"),[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daphne_Guinness#cite_note-WMag-21)[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daphne_Guinness#cite_note-NYTWilson-22) and created an estimated 100 pieces for herself in 2010 with no intention of selling them.[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daphne_Guinness#cite_note-blasberg-23)[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daphne_Guinness#cite_note-24) She designed _Contra Mundum_, an 18-carat white gold glove encrusted with diamonds, with British jeweler [Shaun Leane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shaun_Leane "Shaun Leane") and Alexander McQueen.[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daphne_Guinness#cite_note-Vogue2020-25)[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daphne_Guinness#cite_note-VogueLeane-26) The glove was worn in McQueen's shows, and was auctioned at Sotheby's in 2017.[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daphne_Guinness#cite_note-NYTSothebys-27)

She was named to the [International Best Dressed List](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Best_Dressed_List "International Best Dressed List") Hall of Fame in 1994.[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daphne_Guinness#cite_note-NYTBestDressed-28)[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daphne_Guinness#cite_note-29) Guinness has styled photo shoots for photographers [Steven Klein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steven_Klein_/(artist/) "Steven Klein (artist)") and [David LaChappelle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_LaChappelle "David LaChappelle").[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daphne_Guinness#cite_note-WMag-21)

Following a divorce in 1999, Guinness became more involved in the avant-garde fashion movement,[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daphne_Guinness#cite_note-NPRJackiLyden-5) establishing relationships within the fashion industry.[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daphne_Guinness#cite_note-PaperMag2020-30) Guinness was a close friend of the late fashion designer Alexander McQueen[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daphne_Guinness#cite_note-NPRJackiLyden-5)[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daphne_Guinness#cite_note-GuardianDaphne-31) and, according to _Vogue_, she "nurtured" his career.[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daphne_Guinness#cite_note-Vogue2020-25)

In 2004, she was brought on as a fashion consultant for [Gucci](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gucci "Gucci") by [François-Henri Pinault](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fran%C3%A7ois-Henri_Pinault "François-Henri Pinault").[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daphne_Guinness#cite_note-32)

Following the 2007 death of magazine editor [Isabella Blow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isabella_Blow "Isabella Blow"), Guinness purchased Blow's entire fashion collection, months before it was scheduled to be auctioned by [Christie's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christie%27s "Christie's") in 2010.[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daphne_Guinness#cite_note-NYTFashion-33) In 2014, Guinness exhibited more than 100 pieces of Blow's collection at [Somerset House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somerset_House "Somerset House").[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daphne_Guinness#cite_note-Vogue2020-25)

In 2009, she created a scent named _Daphne_ for Comme des Garçons.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daphne_Guinness#cite_note-WMag-21) Guinness collaborated with [NARS Cosmetics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NARS_Cosmetics "NARS Cosmetics") as the model for the fall 2010 campaign, which included an eyeshadow named after her.[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daphne_Guinness#cite_note-blasberg-23)[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daphne_Guinness#cite_note-Harpers2010-34) In 2011, she released a 21-product makeup line with [MAC Cosmetics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MAC_Cosmetics "MAC Cosmetics") that included blushes, lipsticks and nail polishes.[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daphne_Guinness#cite_note-Harpers2011-35)

She curated an exhibition at the [Fashion Institute of Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fashion_Institute_of_Technology "Fashion Institute of Technology") in 2011 that featured more than 100 contemporary pieces by various designers, including Alexander McQueen, [Chanel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chanel "Chanel"), [Valentino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valentino_/(fashion_house/) "Valentino (fashion house)"), and others, all from her personal couture collection.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daphne_Guinness#cite_note-NPRJackiLyden-5) The exhibit also featured _The Phenomenology of Body_, a short film Guinness directed focused on costumes through the ages.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daphne_Guinness#cite_note-NewYorker-4)

As a tribute to the deaths of Isabella Blow and Alexander McQueen, in 2011 Guinness dressed in public for the [Met Gala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Met_Gala "Met Gala") in a [Barneys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barneys "Barneys") window; she wore a feathered McQueen dress and other pieces from Blow's collection.[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daphne_Guinness#cite_note-NYTHoryn-36)

Guinness has produced and edited three short films:

*   [_Cashback_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cashback_/(film/) "Cashback (film)"), a short film nominated for an Academy Award in 2004, was later made into a feature-length version. Guinness produced this film for the photographer [Sean Ellis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Ellis "Sean Ellis").[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daphne_Guinness#cite_note-garratt-1)

In 2011, Guinness starred in Joe Lally's film, _The Murder of Jean Seberg_.[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daphne_Guinness#cite_note-showstudio.com-37)

At the end of 2011, photographers [Markus Klinko](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Markus_Klinko "Markus Klinko") and [Indrani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indrani_/(photographer/) "Indrani (photographer)"), Guinness, and stylist GK Reid produced _The Legend of Lady White Snake_, a film based on a Chinese legend, where Guinness played the central role of Lady White Snake.[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daphne_Guinness#cite_note-38) [Bernard-Henri Lévy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernard-Henri_L%C3%A9vy "Bernard-Henri Lévy") wrote her dialogue for the film.[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daphne_Guinness#cite_note-39)

In 2012, Guinness starred in _Shakki_,[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daphne_Guinness#cite_note-40) a science fiction short film directed by [Julien Landais](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julien_Landais "Julien Landais").

[David Bowie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Bowie "David Bowie") encouraged Guinness to pursue music, introducing her to [Tony Visconti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Visconti "Tony Visconti"),[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daphne_Guinness#cite_note-LouderThanWar2020-41) who had produced three of her albums as of August 2020.[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daphne_Guinness#cite_note-Vogue2020-25)

### _Optimist in Black_ (2016)

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Daphne_Guinness&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Optimist in Black (2016)")\]

After the deaths of her brother Jasper, mentor [David Bowie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Bowie "David Bowie"), and friends Isabella Blow and Alexander McQueen,[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daphne_Guinness#cite_note-SundayTimes2020a-42) Guinness went to a studio in Ireland, intending to record a cover of the [Bob Dylan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Dylan "Bob Dylan") song "[Desolation Row](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desolation_Row "Desolation Row")". While there, she wrote and recorded original songs which became the basis for her first album, _Optimist in Black_.[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daphne_Guinness#cite_note-WMag2016-43) _Optimist in Black_ was released on 27 May 2016, through private label Agent Anonyme/Absolute.[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daphne_Guinness#cite_note-Vogue2016-44) [\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daphne_Guinness#cite_note-AnOther2016-45) The album was described by Kim Taylor Bennett of [_Vice_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_/(magazine/) "Vice (magazine)") magazine as "drama-pop with a gothic tinge"[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daphne_Guinness#cite_note-Vice2016-46) and by Matthew Schneier of _The New York Times_ as having "a glam-rock-ish, slightly psychedelic flavor".[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daphne_Guinness#cite_note-NYTimes2016-47)

### _Daphne & the Golden Chord_ (2018)

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Daphne_Guinness&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Daphne & the Golden Chord (2018)")\]

In April 2018, Guinness released her second album, _Daphne & the Golden Chord_, also produced by Visconti. The album was recorded on analog tapes at [British Grove Studios](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Grove_Studios "British Grove Studios")[\[48\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daphne_Guinness#cite_note-48) in a three-week session. The band included 58 instrumentalists including timpani, tambourine, and bassoon players.[\[49\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daphne_Guinness#cite_note-Paper2018-49) [Will Hodgkinson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Will_Hodgkinson "Will Hodgkinson") of _The Times_ described the album as "aristocratic glam fuelled by wit, character and a clear and abiding love of rock'n'roll".[\[50\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daphne_Guinness#cite_note-Times2018-50)

Guinness' third album, _Revelations_, was released in August 2020.[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daphne_Guinness#cite_note-SundayTimes2020a-42) Like her prior two albums, it was produced by Visconti. Thomas Barrie of British _[GQ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GQ "GQ")_ said _Revelations_ features "lusher, disco-inflected instrumentation, with flourishes arranged by Visconti in strings, and parts written for more experimental, obscure instruments like the theremin and ocarina".[\[51\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daphne_Guinness#cite_note-GQ2020-51) Guinness collaborated with [David LaChapelle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_LaChapelle "David LaChapelle") on a three-part film series also titled _Revelations_, which featured songs from the album and explored references to the [Book of Revelation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Book_of_Revelation "Book of Revelation").[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daphne_Guinness#cite_note-PaperMag2020-30)[\[52\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daphne_Guinness#cite_note-SundayTimes2020b-52)

Guinness released her fourth album, _Sleep_ on June 21, 2024. The album was recorded at British Grove and [Abbey Road](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abbey_Road_Studios "Abbey Road Studios") studios. It was mixed by Ricky Damian, known for his work with [Lady Gaga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lady_Gaga "Lady Gaga"), [Adele](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adele "Adele"), Georgia Smith, [Dua Lipa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dua_Lipa "Dua Lipa"). Other collaborators on the album included Malcolm Doherty, [Tony Visconti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Visconti "Tony Visconti") (who scored the album's strings), [Guy Pratt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guy_Pratt "Guy Pratt") and [Rob Shirakbari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rob_Shirakbari "Rob Shirakbari"). It also features a 34-piece string section.

The album's singles were also released as remixes, remixed by artists including [Hercules & Love Affair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hercules_%26_Love_Affair "Hercules & Love Affair") and Joe Goddard.

Entertainment website _Culture Fix_ listed _Sleep_ as one of the best albums of 2024, describing it as "a sleek and sophisticated blend of gothic charm, art-pop allure, and esoteric creativity."[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daphne_Guinness#cite_note-53)

Guinness' music career began with the release in 2013 and 2014 of several music videos for songs which would later be included in her first album. These early videos include "Fatal Flaw" (directed by [Nick Knight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Knight_/(photographer/) "Nick Knight (photographer)")) in 2013,[\[54\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daphne_Guinness#cite_note-MTV2013-54) and "Evening in Space", directed by LaChapelle, in 2014.[\[55\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daphne_Guinness#cite_note-MTV2014-55) Jessie Peterson of _MTV News_ said the video took the "fashion world to space". It featured costumes from designers such as [Iris van Herpen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iris_van_Herpen "Iris van Herpen") and [Noritaka Tatehana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noritaka_Tatehana "Noritaka Tatehana").

Guinness also released music video versions for two songs that were on the 2018 _Daphne & the Golden Chord_ album – "Talking to Yourself"[\[56\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daphne_Guinness#cite_note-Billboard2018-56) and "Remember to Breathe".[\[57\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daphne_Guinness#cite_note-VMag2017-57)

Two music videos directed by LaChapelle were released in 2020 for "Hallucinations"[\[52\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daphne_Guinness#cite_note-SundayTimes2020b-52) and "Heaven",[\[58\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daphne_Guinness#cite_note-RollingStone2020-58) two of the songs on the _Revelations_ album.

Guinness collaborated with [Nick Knight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Knight_/(photographer/) "Nick Knight (photographer)") again in 2023 on the video for "Hip Neck Spine", the first single to be taken from her fourth album "Sleep". The video for the follow up single, "Mishima" was directed by Paul Fryer. [David LaChappelle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_LaChappelle "David LaChappelle") directed the videos for two singles from the "Sleep" album - "Volcano"and "Time".

Guinness has walked in two of [Naomi Campbell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naomi_Campbell "Naomi Campbell")'s Fashion for Relief shows to raise funds for disaster victims.[\[59\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daphne_Guinness#cite_note-59) In April 2008, she auctioned off part of her wardrobe, with the proceeds going to a British charity called [Womankind Worldwide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Womankind_Worldwide "Womankind Worldwide"), which deals with issues such as domestic violence.[\[60\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daphne_Guinness#cite_note-60)

In June 2010, Guinness purchased at auction the entire wardrobe of Isabella Blow, her friend who died by suicide in 2007. The lot was purchased prior to an auction, which was arranged at [Christie's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christie%27s "Christie's").[\[61\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daphne_Guinness#cite_note-BritishAuctionChristies-61) She later announced that she would be displaying the wardrobe at [Central Saint Martins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Saint_Martins "Central Saint Martins") and online, as well as starting a foundation to help with mental illness.[\[62\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daphne_Guinness#cite_note-FashionistaDGToExhibit-62) The official show, entitled "_Isabella Blow: Fashion Galore,_" was displayed in November 2013 at [Somerset House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somerset_House "Somerset House") in London.[\[63\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daphne_Guinness#cite_note-63)

In February 2013, Guinness, along with [Baroness Monica von Neumann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monica_von_Neumann "Monica von Neumann") and Lynn Ban, donated a collection of her shoes to the [Museum at Fashion Institute of Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fashion_Institute_of_Technology#The_Museum_at_FIT "Fashion Institute of Technology")'s _Shoe Obsession_ exhibit.[\[64\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daphne_Guinness#cite_note-64)

In 1987, she married [Spyros Niarchos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spyros_Niarchos "Spyros Niarchos"), the second son of [Stavros Niarchos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stavros_Niarchos "Stavros Niarchos").[\[65\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daphne_Guinness#cite_note-65) The couple had three children. Her $39 million settlement, obtained at the time of her 1999 divorce, was added to her Guinness inheritance.[\[66\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daphne_Guinness#cite_note-66)

She lives in London and Manhattan with her three children.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daphne_Guinness#cite_note-garratt-1)

She has been romantically involved with French philosopher [Bernard-Henri Lévy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernard-Henri_L%C3%A9vy "Bernard-Henri Lévy") for a number of years. In the February 2011 issue of _[Harper's Bazaar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harper%27s_Bazaar "Harper's Bazaar")_, Guinness confirmed to journalist [Derek Blasberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derek_Blasberg "Derek Blasberg"): "He is obviously the love of my life".[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daphne_Guinness#cite_note-blasberg-23)[\[67\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daphne_Guinness#cite_note-67)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Articles relating to [banshees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banshee "Banshee") and their depictions. They are female spirits in [Irish folklore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irish_folklore "Irish folklore") who herald the death of a family member, usually by screaming, wailing, shrieking, or [keening](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keening "Keening"). Their name is connected to the mythologically important [tumuli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tumulus "Tumulus") or "mounds" that dot the [Irish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ireland "Ireland") countryside.

An insider's guide to your favourite fashion brands

Lee McQueen (he later changed his name to Alexander) was born in London on March 17, 1969. After leaving school at 16 he worked at two Savile Row tailors, then theatrical costumiers Angels and Bermans, where he perfected the brutally sharp tailoring that would become a trademark. After a short stint at Koji Tatsuno he went to Milan to work as a design assistant for Romeo Gigli.

In 1992, he completed his master's degree in fashion design at Central Saint Martins College of Art and Design in London. His degree collection was bought by fashion critic Isabella Blow.

After graduation, he set up his own label and showed his first women's collection, the Taxi Driver, in 1993. He made headlines with a racy collection called Highland Rape two years later, which showed off models in ripped lace dresses and skirts with dangling string.

In 2000, the Gucci Group bought 51 per cent of his company, allowing him to launch eyewear, fragrances, menswear and bags. Last year, he collaborated with sports giant Puma,a nd his first collection of men's and women's Puma trainers was launched in spring this year. McQueen plans to add a diffusion line, McQ. The range for men and women, out this autumn, will include 1960s-inspired biker jackets, dresses and capes. McQueen remains creative director for the brand.

The look?

Known for his theatrical shows, his collections are romantic, with his signature sharply tailored look. He combines bespoke British tailoring, workmanship of haute couture atelier and the finish of Italian manufacturing.

In McQueen’s universe, no one is merely a victim or a ghost, they are a force. And as always, a McQueen campaign is more than just fashion

Llansteffan Castle looms over the Welsh coastline, enveloped in mist and myth. For the Spring/Summer 2025 campaign, Creative Director Seán McGirr summons the ghostly wail of the banshee, a figure native to Irish folklore. Shot by Glen Luchford, the images capture a cast of characters bound to land, sea, and sky by an unseen, unrelenting force.

![Image 1](https://vmagazine.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/McQueen-SS25-Ad-Campaign-Image-6-scaled.jpg)

Photograph by Glen Luchford

The banshee has long been part of McQueen’s visual lexicon. In his second-ever runway show, Lee Alexander McQueen himself referenced Irish folklore, drawing from tales of wailing spirits said to forewarn of tragedy at sea. Shown at London’s legendary Café de Paris, that early collection strengthened McQueen’s ability to weave storytelling, history, and raw emotion into his designs. Now, decades later, Seán McGirr revisits this folkloric being with a new lens.

![Image 2](https://vmagazine.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/McQueen-SS25-Ad-Campaign-Image-8-scaled.jpg)

Photograph by Glen Luchford

“The banshee was a figure that was very present in my childhood imagination growing up in Ireland, and she has recently taken on new meaning for me,” says McGirr. “She embodies a sense of strident self-expression that resonates now—something freeing that drives connection with others.”

For the collection, textures and silhouettes mimic the mythological creature’s spectral presence. Sharp tailoring that dissolves into frayed lace, shredded organza, and sculpted outerwear. The palette shifts between whites, gray, and blacks, enhanced by flickers of gold and ember-like orange.

![Image 3](https://vmagazine.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/McQueen-SS25-Ad-Campaign-Image-2-scaled.jpg)

Photograph by Glen Luchford

Embellishments refine the silhouette, capturing the depth of a folkloric tale. Delicate beading, dimensional jewelry, and intricate embroidery add layers of texture and meaning to the collection.

# **Alexander McQueen: Savage Beauty**

**May 4 – July 31, 2011**

### **Gallery Text and Labels**


2


**Gallery Text**

**INTRODUCTION**

“I’m a romantic schizophrenic.” Alexander McQueen

Alexander McQueen was a designer whose dazzling creativity and startling
originality were expressed through the technical virtuosity of his fashions and the
conceptual complexity of his runway presentations, suggestive of avant-garde
installation and performance art. His vision of fashion relentlessly questioned and
challenged the requisites of clothing. Rare among designers, he saw beyond
clothing’s physical constraints to its ideational and ideological possibilities. For
McQueen, fashion and politics were linked inexorably, as were fashion and
emotions. Through his runway presentations, McQueen validated powerful
emotions as compelling and undeniable sources of aesthetic experience. Like a
painter or writer of the Romantic Movement, McQueen associated unfettered
emotionalism with the appreciation of beauty. Over and over again, his shows
elicited an uneasy pleasure that merged wonder and terror, incredulity and
revulsion, feelings associated with the Romantic concept of the Sublime. Beyond
the Sublime, however, McQueen engaged deeply with other philosophical
abstractions of the Romantic Movement – individualism, historicism, nationalism,
exoticism, primitivism, and naturalism – which are presented as the dominant
thematics of this exhibition. What comes to light is a vision of fashion that aimed
to reconstitute the Romantic past into the Postmodern present. McQueen once
remarked that he was “overly romantic.” But it was precisely his romantic
yearnings that propelled his creativity and advanced fashion in directions both
unimagined and unprecedented.

Courtesy of Alexander McQueen
